en: Itivuttaka 54 Tikanipāta, Paṭhamavagga Thus it was said by the Blessed One; having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported to the Blessed One what had occurred. "Ānanda, if a bhikkhu should dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, he would understand as it really is: 'This is suffering. He would understand as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering. He would understand as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering. He would understand as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. If a bhikkhu should dwell contemplating feelings in feelings... If a bhikkhu should dwell contemplating mind in mind... If a bhikkhu should dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, he would understand as it really is: 'This is suffering. He would understand as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering. He would understand as it really is:

'This is the cessation of suffering. He would understand as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. "Indeed, Bhante, if a bhikkhu should dwell contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, he would understand as it really is: 'This is suffering'... 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. "It is for this reason, Ānanda, that you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall dwell contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the Venerable Ānanda rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus! "Venerable sir," they replied. The Blessed One said this: "Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a stone, the person who is like a water jar, and the person who is like a lotus. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a stone? Here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is being exhorted and instructed by the Teacher or by a fellow disciple in the Teacher’s presence, he does not listen, does not lend an ear, and does not apply his whole mind to understand; he does not grasp the Dhamma as it is taught and explained. Just as a stone of great size, thrown into a pool of water, sinks and stays at the bottom, so too, when a bhikkhu is being exhorted and instructed... he does not grasp the Dhamma as it is taught and explained. This is called a person who is like a stone. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a water jar? Here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is being exhorted and instructed by the Teacher or by a fellow disciple in the Teacher’s presence, he listens, lends an ear, and applies his whole mind to understand; he grasps the Dhamma as it is taught and explained. But when he has gone away, he quickly forgets it again. Just as a water jar, when filled with water and placed on level ground, leaks and empties out, so too, when a bhikkhu is being exhorted and instructed... he grasps the Dhamma as it is taught and explained, but when he has gone away, he quickly forgets it again. This is called a person who is like a water jar. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a lotus? Here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is being exhorted and instructed by the Teacher or by a fellow disciple in the Teacher’s presence, he listens, lends an ear, and applies his whole mind to understand; he grasps the Dhamma as it is taught and explained. And when he has gone away, he does not quickly forget it, but retains it in mind and masters it. Just as a blue, red, or white lotus, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water, so too, when a bhikkhu is being exhorted and instructed... he grasps the Dhamma as it is taught and explained, and when he has gone away, he does not quickly forget it, but retains it in mind and masters it. This is called a person who is like a lotus. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus have I heard. Thus it was said by the Blessed One; thus have I heard:
The search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, and the search for the holy life—
these, monks, are the three searches.”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
The disciple of the mindful Buddha understands seeking and the origin of seekings.
and the path leading to their destruction—
through the destruction of these searches, a bhikkhu [is liberated].
“Free from hunger, he has attained final Nibbāna.
This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
